newsitem.title: CHINA: China copper industry seen covered to mid-1997.
newsitem.headline: China copper industry seen covered to mid-1997.

text.p: Prospects are fading of a move by China into the copper market, with East Asian metal traders saying Chinese smelters are covered through to the middle of 1997 and in some cases beyond.
Traders polled by Reuters accepted that China's copper stockpile around the beginning of this year amounted to 170,000 tonnes, as reported in the official press.
Low demand and a lack of cash had kept China away from significant copper purchases in recent months, traders said.
That 170,000 tonnes accounted for 17 percent of total annual demand, a supplier source said.
He and other sources have said China's smelters have adequate inventory for the time being, with some, notably Jinlong in central Anhui province, covered to the end of 1997.
The Jinlong copper smelter started operations on April 8, Sumitomo Metal Mining Co, which holds a 20 percent share, said on Tuesday. Itochu Corp has 7.5 percent.

Sumitomo said Jinlong would start producing refined copper in May and turn out 60,000 to 70,000 tonnes by the end of the year. It is due to become China's biggest smelter, with capacity of 100,000 tonnes.
Two shipments of copper had already been delivered to Jinlong, with another five to arrive later in the year, the supplier source said.
"It is true that for the moment it is pretty quiet," another source said of the China market.
Once existing inventory was run down, some buying could be possible, he said, adding, "But what for, if metal demand is not there?"

A European trader noted that while official customs figures showed China's copper imports so far this year had increased sharply on last year, the material was arriving at southern ports and was being absorbed by smelters in the south.
Very little material was heading to smelters in the country's north, he said, adding that the government might be lending to smelters from central reserves as the need arose.

While this could not be confirmed because China regards all information concerning commodity stockpiles as a state secret, China's central reserve authorities were reported to have imported up to 300,000 tonnes of copper in late 1996.
Official figures put total 1996 imports of uncast copper and copper products at 714,248 tonnes, up 32.7 percent on the year before.
Western analysts and industry experts agreed with a figure of 1.417 million tonnes for total Chinese copper supplies in 1996, with 967,000 tonnes of that being imports of scrap, blister and cathode.
The customs figures showed China imported 14,887 tonnes of refined copper and copper anodes for electrolytic refining in the first two months of 1997, up 67.4 percent year-on-year.
Imports in February alone were 8,429 tonnes.
Copper waste and scrap imports were 75,868 tonnes in the first two months, up 10.8 percent on the same period in 1996, with February imports alone at 37,528 tonnes.
Those imports had been arriving in small lots, ordered by Chinese trading houses to sell directly to smelters, traders said.
With the world price of copper hovering around $2,300 a tonne since early in 1997, the market was too high for the notoriously price-sensitive Chinese, they added.
But the sluggish market was a more fundamental factor than price, traders throughout the region said.
"I've been saying for a long time that we won't see the Chinese in the market, and not only because the price is high -- they just don't need it," a trader in Singapore said.
-- Shanghai newsroom (86-21) 6279-8544
